stem: A large pull request touches 40 files. The team wants both (a) style and correctness issues local to each file caught, and (b) issues that only show up when comparing how files interact, like a renamed function that one file updated but another didn't. An engineer proposes reviewing each file once, checking for both local and cross-file issues in the same pass. Why will this likely miss issues?
explanation: A per-file pass structurally can't see across files — it has no visibility into how a change in one file interacts with another. The recommended approach splits this into a parallel per-file pass for local issues plus a separate, sequential cross-file integration pass that can see the whole picture at once.

choices.text: A single per-file pass can't see across files, so cross-file interaction issues get missed
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented split exactly — local issues are parallelizable per file, but cross-file issues require a distinct pass that sees the whole picture, which a per-file-only review structurally cannot provide.

choices.text: It won't miss anything, since reviewing each file thoroughly always catches issues from every other file too
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: thoroughness within one file doesn't grant visibility into other files' content — cross-file consistency issues require comparing multiple files directly.

choices.text: The only problem is that this approach uses too many tokens, not that it misses issues
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the core problem is a structural blind spot (no cross-file visibility), not primarily a token-cost concern.

choices.text: This approach only fails if the pull request has fewer than 10 files
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the structural blind spot (no visibility across files within a single per-file pass) applies regardless of file count, not just below some threshold.

choices.text: This approach only fails if run through the Batch API
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: whether requests run via Batch or real-time doesn't change the structural fact that a per-file pass can't see across files.

choices.text: It won't miss anything as long as the reviewing subagent has every tool available
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: tool breadth doesn't grant cross-file visibility; the issue is the review's scope (one file at a time), not which tools it has access to.

stem: A subagent tasked with extracting line items from a scanned invoice returns `{"error": true}` with nothing else. The coordinator has no idea whether the scan was unreadable, the schema didn't match, or something else entirely went wrong, so it can't decide whether retrying, requesting a rescan, or escalating is appropriate. What should the subagent's error response have included?
explanation: Subagents should return structured failure context: what was attempted, why it failed, any partial results, and whether it's worth retrying with a different approach — a bare boolean error flag gives the coordinator nothing to act on.

choices.text: Structured detail — what was attempted, why it failed, and whether retrying is worth it
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is exactly the documented recommended shape, and it directly resolves the coordinator's stated dilemma — enough detail to choose between retry, rescan, or escalation.

choices.text: Nothing more is needed — a bare boolean error flag is sufficient for the coordinator to decide what to do
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly the scenario's stated problem — the coordinator has no basis to choose between retry, rescan, or escalation from a bare flag alone.

choices.text: The subagent's full internal chain-of-thought, unfiltered
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: unfiltered reasoning isn't the structured, actionable failure shape needed; it's noisy and doesn't clearly convey what was attempted, why it failed, or retry viability.

choices.text: A retry request sent automatically without any explanation of what went wrong
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: automatically retrying blind, without diagnosing what went wrong, risks repeating the same failure (e.g. an unreadable scan will fail identically on retry).

choices.text: A generic message reading only "processing failed, please try again later"
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this gives no specific detail about what was attempted or why it failed, leaving the coordinator unable to distinguish a rescan-worthy issue from a schema mismatch.

choices.text: The document's raw binary content, unmodified
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: dumping the raw document back doesn't explain what specifically went wrong during extraction or whether retrying makes sense.

stem: Four parallel subagents each research a different aspect of a market report. Three return findings shaped as `{"summary": str, "citations": list[str]}`, but the fourth — built by a different engineer — returns a long free-form paragraph with citations embedded inline as prose. What problem does this create for the coordinator, and what's the fix?
explanation: Parallel execution requires a uniform output shape across subagents so the coordinator can synthesize results generically. A subagent returning a different, free-form shape forces the coordinator to special-case it, undermining the reliability of automated synthesis — the fix is standardizing all four subagents' output to the same structured shape.

choices.text: The mismatched shape forces special-casing; standardize all four subagents' output
choices.reasoning: Correct: uniform output shape across parallel subagents is what lets the coordinator synthesize generically — a lone free-form output breaks that and requires special handling, which the fix eliminates by standardizing.

choices.text: There's no real problem, since the coordinator can read prose just as well as structured JSON
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while a coordinator could parse prose, it undermines the ability to synthesize generically across all four subagents' results the way a uniform shape allows, and reintroduces per-subagent special-casing.

choices.text: The fix is to have the coordinator ignore the fourth subagent's findings entirely
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: discarding legitimate research findings over a formatting mismatch wastes real work; standardizing the output shape is the appropriate fix, not discarding the content.

choices.text: The fix is to give the fourth subagent a higher-tier model so its prose is better written
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: improving prose quality doesn't address the actual problem, which is shape inconsistency for automated synthesis, not writing quality.

choices.text: The fix is to switch all four subagents to the Batch API to normalize their output automatically
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: batch processing doesn't normalize or standardize response content shape; that's a schema/prompt design decision, not a property of which API mode is used.

choices.text: The fix is to merge all four subagents into a single subagent to avoid shape mismatches
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: merging discards the benefit of independent parallel research; the actual fix is standardizing each subagent's output shape, not eliminating parallelism.

stem: A support coordinator dispatches to two subagent roles: a "lookup" subagent (given order-search and knowledge-base-search tools) and an "action" subagent (given refund-issue and account-update tools). An engineer proposes merging both roles into one subagent with all four tools, arguing it would simplify the architecture. What consideration should weigh against this?
explanation: Keeping subagents narrow — roughly 4-5 tools scoped to a specific role — reduces tool-selection complexity and role drift. Merging a read-only lookup role with a mutating action role into one subagent with all four tools increases the chance the model reaches for the wrong tool (e.g. issuing a refund during what should be a lookup-only interaction).

choices.text: Merging lookup and action tools raises the risk of an unintended mutating action during a lookup step
choices.reasoning: Correct: this reflects the documented concern about broadening a subagent's toolset beyond its role — mixing read-only and mutating capabilities in one role increases the risk of the wrong tool being selected at the wrong time.

choices.text: There's no meaningful downside; merging is always simpler and strictly better
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this ignores the documented role-drift risk that comes from broadening a subagent's toolset beyond a single, narrow purpose.

choices.text: The only concern is increased token cost from having four tools defined instead of two per subagent
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while token cost is a minor factor, the primary documented concern is tool-selection complexity and role drift, not raw token count of tool definitions.

choices.text: Merging is fine as long as the merged subagent uses a higher-tier model
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier doesn't eliminate the tool-selection complexity introduced by mixing read-only and mutating tools in one role.

choices.text: Merging is fine as long as it happens after refund and account-update tools are marked destructiveHint: true
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: annotation hints are advisory metadata, not enforced restrictions — marking a tool destructiveHint doesn't prevent the model from selecting it inappropriately.

choices.text: The only consideration is whether the two roles are parallelizable, which is irrelevant here
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: parallelizability isn't the issue being raised — the concern is about tool-selection complexity and role drift from combining a lookup role with an action role.

stem: A pipeline extracts financial figures from vendor documents and auto-approves payments under $500 without human review, per a system-prompt instruction: "only auto-approve payments below $500." An audit finds several $600-$800 payments were auto-approved because the model occasionally misread the extracted total. What structural change would have prevented this specific class of error?
explanation: A dollar threshold like this is a hard compliance rule and belongs in code — a threshold check performed by the tool/application itself, not as an instruction to the model to "check the amount is under $X." Enforcing the check at the tool layer means it can't be bypassed by a model misreading or misapplying the instruction.

choices.text: Move the $500 threshold check into the tool itself, so it can't auto-approve over the limit
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is the code-level enforcement pattern — the threshold check happens in the tool, not as something the model is trusted to apply correctly, eliminating this class of misreading-driven error.

choices.text: Reword the system-prompt instruction to be more emphatic about the $500 limit
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a more emphatic instruction is still guidance the model could apply incorrectly if it misreads the extracted amount — the same failure mode as before.

choices.text: Lower the auto-approval threshold to $100 so fewer payments are affected by any misreading
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this reduces exposure but doesn't fix the underlying defect — a model misreading a total could still cause an incorrect auto-approval above whatever threshold is set, just less often.

choices.text: Add more few-shot examples of correctly reading financial totals from documents
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: few-shot examples improve accuracy probabilistically but don't provide the structural guarantee a code-level threshold check does for a hard compliance rule.

choices.text: Switch to a higher-tier model for this extraction task
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a stronger model reduces but doesn't eliminate misreading risk; the compliance-critical threshold should be enforced in code regardless of model capability.

choices.text: Require the model to double-check its own reading of the amount before proceeding
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: self-checking is still guidance-based and can fail the same way the original read did; a code-level enforced check doesn't depend on the model catching its own mistake.

stem: A pipeline runs static analysis on 25 independent microservices, one repo each, with no service's analysis depending on another's results. It's currently implemented as one coordinator that analyzes each repo sequentially, one Task call at a time, taking almost an hour to complete. Which change most directly addresses the runtime, and why?
explanation: Since the 25 analyses are fully independent, issuing the Task calls in parallel within a single coordinator turn (or a bounded number of batches) collapses elapsed time toward the duration of the slowest single repo's analysis rather than the sum of all 25 sequential runs.

choices.text: Launch the independent per-repo analyses as parallel subagents instead of sequentially
choices.reasoning: Correct: independent workstreams are exactly the parallel-subagents use case, and switching from sequential to parallel launch collapses elapsed time to roughly the slowest single analysis instead of the sum of all 25.

choices.text: Switch the pipeline to the Batch API to cut the per-request cost in half
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: Batch reduces cost but has no SLA and up to 24-hour turnaround with no tool-calling within a batch request — unsuitable for a CI pipeline that needs results promptly, and doesn't address the described runtime problem the way parallelization does.

choices.text: Add routing so each repo is classified before analysis begins
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: there's no described classification decision needed here — all 25 repos get the same kind of static analysis; routing doesn't address the sequential-execution bottleneck.

choices.text: Merge all 25 repos' analysis into a single Task call covering everything at once
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this would create one enormous, unwieldy task instead of leveraging the repos' independence for clean parallel execution, and risks exceeding practical context limits.

choices.text: Give the coordinator a higher-tier model so each sequential analysis completes faster
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a faster model per call reduces but doesn't eliminate the fundamental sequential-sum problem; parallel launch addresses the actual architectural cause of the near-hour runtime.

choices.text: Reduce the number of tools available to the coordinator to speed up tool selection
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: tool-selection speed isn't the bottleneck described; the runtime issue is sequential execution of independent work, not tool-list size.

stem: A long-running migration pipeline agent periodically checkpoints its state to survive a pipeline restart. The current checkpoint format stores only a single field: `"last_message": "..."` containing the assistant's most recent reply text. After a restart, the resumed agent frequently repeats work it had already completed. What is most likely wrong with the checkpoint design?
explanation: A single free-text field carries none of the structure needed to know what's already done — the recommended pattern is a structured export (completed_steps, open_gaps, key decisions) so a resumed run can pick up exactly where it left off instead of re-deriving or repeating prior work from an ambiguous text snippet.

choices.text: The checkpoint lacks structured fields like completed_steps, so the resumed agent repeats work
choices.reasoning: Correct: a bare last-message string doesn't encode which steps are complete versus still open, which is exactly why the resumed agent can't reliably avoid repeating finished work — the fix is the documented structured-export pattern.

choices.text: The checkpoint should instead store the entire raw conversation transcript in full
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a full raw transcript is explicitly what the guidance recommends against for resumption; it's inefficient and still doesn't clearly separate completed steps from open ones without significant re-parsing.

choices.text: The checkpoint format is fine; the problem must be a bug in the pipeline's restart mechanism
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the described symptom (repeating already-completed work) is a direct, predictable consequence of a checkpoint that doesn't record completed steps — no separate restart bug is needed to explain it.

choices.text: The checkpoint should store only a numeric progress percentage instead of any text
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a bare percentage still doesn't tell the resumed agent specifically which steps are done and which remain open — it lacks the same structural detail as the current design.

choices.text: The checkpoint needs to store the model's internal weights at the time of interruption
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model weights aren't something an application checkpoints per-task; the missing piece is structured task-progress state, not the model itself.

choices.text: The checkpoint is unrelated to the repeated-work symptom; the issue must be an outdated model version
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model version has no bearing on whether a resumed agent knows what work was already completed — that information comes entirely from what the checkpoint records.

stem: An extraction pipeline's subagents each report a claim as extracted, with no indication of which source document, page, or extraction pass produced it. A downstream audit needs to verify a specific figure against its original document but has no way to trace it back. What requirement, if enforced from the start, would have prevented this?
explanation: Provenance — attaching source id, date, methodology, and confidence to every claim — is what allows a later reviewer to trace a claim back to its origin and verify or challenge it. Without it, an audit has no path back to the original document.

choices.text: Requiring every extracted claim to carry provenance — source id, location, and methodology
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is exactly the missing requirement; without provenance attached at extraction time, there's no reliable path back to the original document for later verification.

choices.text: Requiring the pipeline to run on the highest-tier model available
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: model tier doesn't create a traceability path back to source documents; that requires explicit provenance metadata attached to each claim.

choices.text: Requiring the pipeline to use the Batch API instead of real-time processing
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: batch versus real-time is a latency/cost tradeoff and has no bearing on whether claims carry source traceability information.

choices.text: Requiring a single aggregate confidence score across the entire extracted document
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a document-level aggregate score still wouldn't let the auditor trace one specific figure back to its exact source location.

choices.text: Nothing could have prevented this; source traceability isn't achievable in an automated extraction pipeline
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: attaching provenance metadata at extraction time is exactly the documented, achievable fix for this class of traceability gap.

choices.text: Requiring the extraction schema to use strict enums with no escape-hatch category
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: enum strictness relates to reducing fabrication in categorical fields, not to tracing a claim back to its source document.
